vignette:
She is 51, a South Eastern Asian woman who has spent most of her adult life learning how to make other people feel safe. In her dental practice, she is known for her steady hands and calming voice. Patients who come in embarrassed, fearful, or in pain often relax when she explains each step before she begins. She likes order, clean lines, predictable instruments laid out in their proper places. For years, that structure feels like a refuge. At home, she is married, practical, attentive to routines, someone who keeps the family calendar in her head.

The trouble begins so quietly that she doubts herself at first. A man who had come to the clinic a handful of times starts lingering after appointments. At first he asks questions that seem merely awkward-whether she is always in on Thursdays, whether she drives herself home, whether she lives nearby. She redirects him politely. Then flowers arrive at the front desk without a card. A week later, her receptionist mentions that the same patient has called twice to ask if the doctor is working late. He begins requesting appointments he does not seem to need. During one visit, he stares at her in a way that makes her skin tighten. She finishes the procedure, removes her gloves, and realizes her heart is pounding.

She tells herself not to overreact. She has spent a lifetime being careful, courteous, not making trouble. But the man's presence begins spreading into the edges of her day. She notices him parked across the street from the clinic. She sees a figure she thinks is him near the grocery store. He sends messages to the office email that are personal, admiring, insistent. When the staff blocks one address, another appears. He comments on details he should not know-that she wore blue on Tuesday, that she left the office after dark, that her husband was out of town for a conference. Reading that message, she feels a coldness move through her chest and down her arms. After that, every ordinary part of her life seems to lose its innocence.

Her husband urges her to report it, and eventually she does. By then she is already sleeping lightly, waking at sounds she would once have ignored-the gate clicking, tires slowing outside, footsteps in the corridor of their apartment building. She checks the locks repeatedly before bed, then again after she has already lain down. In the clinic, she asks staff to walk her to her car. She changes her route home, then changes it again when she starts imagining she is being followed. At red lights she scans the rearview mirror and memorizes license plates. She hates the feeling of becoming suspicious of everyone, but she cannot stop.

The harassment continues in bursts. Some weeks there is silence, and she starts to believe it may be over. Then a note is left on her windshield, or the clinic receives another message, or she catches sight of a familiar car and the whole fear rushes back as if no time has passed. Her body begins reacting before her mind can reason with it. Her jaw clenches while she is drilling a tooth. Sweat gathers under her mask. Once, when a male patient suddenly stands up from the dental chair before she expects it, she recoils so sharply that both of them freeze. Afterward she hides in her office and cries in a way that feels humiliating and strangely distant, as if she is watching herself from outside the room.

At home she tries not to burden her husband with the full extent of it, but he notices how much smaller her world has become. She used to stay late to finish charts; now she leaves before dusk whenever she can. She used to enjoy stopping for tea after work; now she goes nowhere alone unless necessary. She closes the curtains before evening. If her husband is late, she calls him repeatedly, then feels angry when he sounds puzzled. She knows he is not the danger, but her nerves do not seem to care about logic. Intimacy becomes difficult too. When he touches her unexpectedly from behind in the kitchen, she startles violently, then feels guilty when she sees his face.

What troubles her most is not only the fear but the erosion of the person she thought she was. She has always been composed, competent, someone younger dentists come to for advice. Now she loses her train of thought during consultations. She rereads patient notes and still cannot absorb them. She avoids looking at certain cars, certain men in waiting rooms, certain corners near the clinic entrance. At night she has vivid dreams in which she is trying to lock doors that will not stay shut, or she is back in the operatory and realizes the stalker has been sitting there all along. She wakes with her heart racing, already listening.

In quieter moments, she understands that much of her day is organized around not feeling afraid, and yet fear is present anyway. She still goes to work, still leans over patients with the same careful precision, still answers questions in her reassuring voice. But underneath, she is braced. Even now, months later, she enters every room by first noting the exits, every phone call by wondering how the caller got the number, every unexpected shadow by preparing, for one instant, to run.
